281.title: The mystics in you
281.hook: mystics aren't a different species; they paid attention for a long time
281.howItsDone: Many Christians of every church read the mystics as companions in prayer, and practice daily periods of quiet attention, such as silent prayer, slow scripture reading, or doing ordinary work with God in mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Seraphim of Sarov: my joy, Christ is risen. Your line was acquire peace. Who did you greet like a joy? Day two hundred eighty-one.

When people hear the word mystic, they often picture someone floating a few inches off the floor. Glowing eyes. Visions every Tuesday. Someone who is simply built differently from the rest of us. But look at who we've actually met these twenty days. A soldier with a limp who cooked dinner. A dyer's daughter. A sick woman in a small room. A monk who copied books. A young man who couldn't find a minister to help him. A nun who didn't know how to begin her book. Not a different species. Ordinary people. So what made them mystics? Today's word: mystic.
screen: `FLOATING OFF THE FLOOR?` → `A COOK, A DYER'S DAUGHTER.` → `NOT A DIFFERENT SPECIES.`

segments.voice: The word mystic comes from Greek. It shares a root with mystery, and goes back to a verb that means to close, to close the eyes or the lips. In the early church, mystical didn't mean spooky. It meant hidden: the hidden meaning inside scripture, the hidden life of God inside the bread and wine, the hidden depth inside an ordinary life. A mystic, in that old sense, is someone who has learned to see what's hidden in plain sight. And how did they learn? Look back at the whole stretch. The abbas and ammas said: give me a word, tend the fire, go to your cell and stay put. Gregory said: always further in. Benedict said: pray and work, and treat the pots like altar vessels. Hildegard saw greening. Bernard mapped four loves. Francis called the sun his brother. The Cloud said: reached by love. Julian, the anchoress, saw the hazelnut and heard that all shall be well. Catherine spoke up. The Imitation said: follow quietly. Teresa found a room further in; John found that dark is not absent. Brother Lawrence found God among the pots. Fox found that of God in everyone. Seraphim acquired peace. Under all of it runs one thread. They paid attention. To God, to scripture, to the people in front of them, to the ordinary thing in their hands. Not for a minute. For years. The Psalm puts it in five words: "Be still, and know that I am God." Christians have always said that seeing God is a gift, not something you can earn or force. But the mystics would all agree on where the door opens. It opens when you're looking.
screen: `MYSTIC: TO CLOSE THE EYES.` · `HIDDEN IN PLAIN SIGHT.` · `TWENTY DAYS, ONE THREAD.` · `BE STILL, AND KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay attention. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing in front of you: your hand, a cup, the light on the wall. Look at it as if you'd never seen it before. When your mind wanders, and it will, bring it back, like the monks did, without fuss. That's all the mystics ever did, over and over, for years. If you pray, you can simply be still, and know. The bell holds the time.
Mystic. From a Greek word about closing the eyes: someone who learns to see what's hidden in plain sight.

Your line: attention is the beginning. Today, give five whole minutes of attention to one thing or one person. No phone. That's the end of the mystics. Tomorrow, the family of churches. Day two hundred eighty-one.

282.title: One church, then many
282.hook: for a thousand years there was broadly one church, with arguments; then came divisions
282.howItsDone: Many Christians pray each January during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity, and churches of different traditions often worship together at ecumenical services, while keeping their own practices.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was mystic, someone who learns to see what's hidden in plain sight. Your line was attention is the beginning. What did five minutes of attention show you? Day two hundred eighty-two.

Drive through almost any town and count the churches. Catholic on one corner. Baptist across the street. Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal, a Greek Orthodox church with a dome, a storefront with a hand-painted sign. If you didn't grow up inside one, it can be confusing. Aren't they all Christian? Why so many? It's a fair question, and Christians ask it too, sometimes with real sadness. Over the next couple of weeks we'll meet this family of churches one by one, each described the way it describes itself. Today we start at the beginning, with the family tree. Today's word: one church.
screen: `COUNT THE CHURCHES.` → `WHY SO MANY?` → `THE FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: For roughly the first thousand years, Christians broadly thought of themselves as one church. Not one building or one boss, but one family, spread across the Roman world, with great centers at Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem. It was never a quiet family. There were fierce arguments, and some real early separations: after a council in 451, several ancient churches, including the Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian and Syriac churches, went their own way, and they're still here today. But the big split most people mean came later. Over centuries, the Greek-speaking East and the Latin-speaking West grew apart: different languages, different customs, arguments over the pope's authority and over a phrase in the creed. In 1054, envoys from Rome and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other. The break hardened over the centuries after, and became what we now call the Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church. Then, in 1517, a German monk named Martin Luther posted his objections to practices in the Western church, and the Protestant Reformation began. Out of it came Lutherans, Reformed and Presbyterian churches, Anglicans, Anabaptists, and later Baptists, Methodists, Pentecostals and many more. Paul, writing long before any of this, used a picture Christians keep coming back to. In the King James Bible: "For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ." And: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." In 1965, the pope and the patriarch of Constantinople lifted the excommunications of 1054. The divisions remain. So does the longing.
screen: `A THOUSAND YEARS, BROADLY ONE.` · `451: THE ANCIENT EASTERN CHURCHES.` · `1054: EAST AND WEST.` · `1517: THE REFORMATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of one church that isn't your own, or, if you don't belong to one, a church you've driven past. Picture its doors on a Sunday morning, the people walking in: families, old couples, someone alone. If you pray, you can pray for them, in whatever words come. If you don't, just wish them well. Hold them for a moment as part of one family. The bell holds the time.
One church. How Christians broadly saw themselves for a thousand years, before the divisions, and what many still long for.
Your line: one body, many parts. Today, when you pass a church, any church, notice it, and remember it's part of one very big, very complicated family. Day two hundred eighty-two.

283.title: The councils
283.hook: bishops met at Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451) to settle who Jesus is
283.tomorrow: the ancient churches of the east
283.howItsDone: Many churches, Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and others, say the Nicene Creed together at the main Sunday service, usually standing, after the readings and sermon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one church, then many: a thousand years of broadly one church, with arguments, and then the splits. Your line was one body many parts. Which church not your own did you hold in mind? Day two hundred eighty-three.

Picture the year 325, in a lakeside town called Nicaea, in what is now Turkey. Around three hundred bishops arrive, some on imperial horses, paid for by the emperor Constantine. A few of them carry scars. Only a dozen years earlier, Christians were being arrested and tortured, and some of these old men still limp from it. Now the emperor has called them together, because the church is arguing so loudly it can be heard in the marketplace. A priest from Alexandria named Arius has been teaching that the Son of God was created, the first and greatest of all creatures, but a creature. People are setting his ideas to catchy songs. Others are furious. So the bishops sit down in one room to answer a question that sounds simple: who is Jesus? Today's word is the room.
screen: `NICAEA, THE YEAR 325.` → `BISHOPS WITH SCARS.` → `WHO IS JESUS?`

segments.voice: A council is a gathering of church leaders to settle something together. The Greek word is synodos, a way taken together, the root of our word synod. The idea goes back to the Bible itself: in Acts 15 the apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem to argue about whether new believers must keep the Jewish law, and they send out a letter that begins, it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us. At Nicaea, the bishops rejected Arius. They wrote a statement saying the Son is of one being with the Father, one Greek word, homoousios. Fifty-six years later, a second council, at Constantinople, expanded it into the creed most churches still say, known as the Nicene Creed. In the old English of the Book of Common Prayer it says the Son is "God of God, Light of Light, Very God of very God, Begotten, not made." Then in 451, at Chalcedon, another council asked the next question: if Jesus is truly God, is he truly human too? Their answer was yes, one person, two natures, not mixed and not split. We'll come back to that one. Two things are worth knowing. First, the councils didn't invent faith in Jesus; they tried to put into words what churches were already praying and singing, and they argued fiercely doing it, with politics mixed in. Second, not everyone accepted every council. Chalcedon, especially, led to a lasting split, which is tomorrow's story. And notice how the council's creed began: not I believe, but we believe.
screen: `SYNODOS: A WAY TAKEN TOGETHER.` · `NICAEA: OF ONE BEING WITH THE FATHER.` · `CHALCEDON: TRULY GOD, TRULY HUMAN.` · `NOT EVERYONE AGREED.` · then, large: `BEGOTTEN, NOT MADE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the Nicene Creed once. You can find it in almost any prayer book, or online. Read it slowly, the way you'd read a letter from someone who had suffered to write it. Notice which line stops you: the one you love, or the one you don't understand. If you pray, you can say it aloud. If you don't, just read it as a very old answer to a very old question. Then settle, breathe, and let that one line sit with you. The bell holds the time.
Council. Church leaders gathered to settle a question together. From Jerusalem to Nicaea to Chalcedon.
Your line: we believe. Today, notice one thing you believe that you didn't work out alone, something you were handed by people who came before. Day two hundred eighty-three.

284.title: The ancient churches of the east
284.hook: Copts, Ethiopians, Armenians and Syriacs keep some of the oldest Christian traditions on earth
284.howItsDone: Oriental Orthodox Christians worship in ancient liturgical languages such as Coptic, Ge'ez, Armenian and Syriac, keep long fasts through the year, and many stand through services that last several hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the councils: Nicaea and Chalcedon, bishops trying to say who Jesus is. Your line was we believe. What belief did you notice you'd been handed? Day two hundred eighty-four.

In the highlands of northern Ethiopia there's a town called Lalibela, where, many centuries ago, whole churches were carved down into the solid red rock. Not built. Carved, from the top down, like sculptures you can walk into. On a feast day before dawn, thousands of people in white shawls fill the trenches around them, and priests chant in Ge'ez, a language nobody speaks at the market anymore, but everyone there knows by heart in prayer. Drums. Sistrums, little rattles like the ones in the Bible. Swaying. If you've only ever pictured Christianity in a European cathedral or an American strip-mall church, this is a surprise: some of the oldest Christian traditions on earth are African and Asian. Today's word is their family name.
screen: `LALIBELA: CHURCHES CARVED FROM ROCK.` → `CHANTING IN GE'EZ.` → `OLDER THAN YOU THINK.`

segments.voice: The Oriental Orthodox churches are a family of six: the Coptic church of Egypt, the Ethiopian and Eritrean churches, the Armenian Apostolic church, the Syriac Orthodox church, and the Malankara church in India. Oriental here just means eastern. They're called Orthodox, but they're a separate family from the Greek and Russian Orthodox you may know. Here's why. Remember Chalcedon, in 451, and its formula: Christ in two natures. These churches didn't accept that wording. They held to an older phrase from Cyril of Alexandria: one nature of God the Word made flesh, divine and human united, never mixed and never divided. Others called them monophysites, one-nature people, a label they reject. They call themselves miaphysite: one united nature. For centuries each side thought the other had lost something essential. Then, in the late twentieth century, theologians from these churches, the Eastern Orthodox and the Catholic Church sat down together and agreed, in joint statements, that much of the split had been about words, and that they share far more than they thought. Their roots run deep. Armenia is remembered as the first kingdom to make Christianity its official faith, in the early 300s. The Ethiopian church loves the story in Acts 8 of an Ethiopian official baptized on a desert road, and a line from the Psalms: "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God." Coptic, their old church language, descends from the language of the pharaohs. Syriac is a close cousin of the Aramaic Jesus spoke. These churches have lived through empires, massacres and exile. Many of their people are refugees today. And every Sunday, they still sing.
screen: `SIX CHURCHES, ONE FAMILY.` · `ONE UNITED NATURE: MIAPHYSITE.` · `AN ARGUMENT PARTLY ABOUT WORDS.` · `STILL SINGING, THROUGH EVERYTHING.` · then, large: `ETHIOPIA SHALL SOON STRETCH OUT HER HANDS UNTO GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one fact about the Ethiopian church, and let it sit. Here's one to start with. Every Ethiopian Orthodox church keeps a tabot, a carved tablet standing for the ark of the covenant, wrapped in cloth, and a church isn't a church without one. Settle, and breathe. Picture those white shawls before dawn. Picture people who have kept one way of praying for over sixteen hundred years. If you pray, you can pray for these churches, and for their people who are far from home. If you don't, just hold them in mind with respect. The bell holds the time.
Oriental Orthodox. The six ancient churches of Egypt, Ethiopia, Eritrea, Armenia, Syria and India, who kept their own way after Chalcedon.
Your line: very old, still singing. Today, find a piece of Coptic, Armenian or Ethiopian church music and listen for one minute. Day two hundred eighty-four.

285.title: The Church of the East
285.hook: Christians who traveled the Silk Road to China and India in the first millennium
285.howItsDone: The Assyrian Church of the East and its sister churches still pray in Syriac, keep an ancient liturgy called the Liturgy of Addai and Mari, and honor the cross without a figure on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Oriental Orthodox: Copts, Ethiopians, Armenians, Syriacs and the Malankara church. Your line was very old still singing. Did you find a minute of their music? Day two hundred eighty-five.

In 1625, workers digging near the city of Xi'an, in China, pulled a huge stone slab out of the ground. It stood taller than a man, with a cross carved at the top, rising out of a lotus flower. Below it, nearly two thousand Chinese characters, and a border of writing in Syriac. The stone had been set up in the year 781. It told how a monk named Alopen had arrived at the Tang emperor's capital in 635, carrying scriptures, and how the emperor had welcomed him, had the books translated, and let him build a monastery. Christians in China, in the 600s. Most people who hear this for the first time are startled. It's a story many Western Christians never learned. Today's word is the church that walked there.
screen: `A STONE FROM THE YEAR 781.` → `A CROSS RISING FROM A LOTUS.` → `CHRISTIANS IN CHINA, 635.`

segments.voice: The Church of the East grew up in Persia, beyond the Roman Empire's eastern border, among Christians who prayed in Syriac, a cousin of Jesus's own Aramaic. Its leader, the catholicos, sat in Seleucia-Ctesiphon, near modern Baghdad. Because it lay outside Rome, it went its own way on the councils. Westerners long called it Nestorian, after a bishop condemned in 431, but that's a label the church didn't choose, and many today find it misleading. Now picture the Silk Road: caravans, oases, monasteries along the way. Merchants and monks from this church carried the gospel along it, across Central Asia to China, and down to India, where the Saint Thomas Christians trace their faith to the apostle Thomas himself. In China they called their faith the luminous teaching. At its height, around the year 1300, this one church stretched from the Mediterranean to the Pacific, with more territory than any church in Europe. A monk from near Beijing, Rabban Sauma, even traveled west and met the pope and the king of France, in 1287. Then came centuries of hardship: plagues, conquests, the collapse of the Mongol empire, massacres. The church shrank almost to nothing in China and Central Asia. Its heirs today, the Assyrian Church of the East, the Ancient Church of the East, and churches in communion with Rome such as the Chaldeans, are small, many of them refugees from Iraq and Syria. Jesus told his friends in Acts that they would be his witnesses "unto the uttermost part of the earth." Most maps of Christian history draw that line going west. This church reminds you it went east too, early and far.
screen: `A CHURCH BEYOND ROME, IN PERSIA.` · `A LABEL IT DIDN'T CHOOSE.` · `ALONG THE SILK ROAD TO CHINA.` · `SMALL NOW, MANY OF THEM REFUGEES.` · then, large: `UNTO THE UTTERMOST PART OF THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a map of Asia. On your phone is fine. Find Baghdad. Then trace a finger east, across Iran, over the mountains of Central Asia, all the way to Xi'an in China. Then back, and down to Kerala, on India's southwest coast. That's thousands of miles, walked by monks and merchants more than a thousand years ago. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can pray for the Christians who still live along that road, and for those who had to leave it. If you don't, just let the size of the map sink in. The bell holds the time.
The Church of the East. The Syriac-speaking church of Persia that carried the gospel along the Silk Road to China and India.

segments.voice: Your line: the road went east. Today, when you picture Christian history, add one line on the map that goes the other way. Day two hundred eighty-five.

286.hook: East and West split, over authority and a word in the creed, with faults on both sides
286.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox leaders now meet regularly, and every year on the feasts of Saint Andrew and of Saints Peter and Paul delegations from Rome and Constantinople visit each other to pray together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Church of the East, monks and merchants on the Silk Road. Your line was the road went east. Did you trace that road on a map? Day two hundred eighty-six.

July, 1054. Constantinople, the great church of Hagia Sophia, in the middle of the afternoon service. Three envoys from the pope in Rome walk up the aisle, led by a cardinal named Humbert, and lay a document on the altar. It excommunicates the patriarch of Constantinople. Then they walk out, shaking the dust off their feet. A deacon runs after them, begging them to take it back. They refuse. Days later the patriarch, Michael Cerularius, excommunicates the envoys in return. And here's the strange part: the pope who sent them had already died, so some historians wonder whether the document even counted. Nobody in that church knew they were watching the start of something that would last nearly a thousand years. Today's word is what happened.
screen: `HAGIA SOPHIA, JULY 1054.` → `A PAPER ON THE ALTAR.` → `EXCOMMUNICATION, BOTH WAYS.`

segments.voice: Schism comes from the Greek schisma, a tear, a rip in cloth. Jesus uses it in a saying about sewing new cloth onto an old coat: "the rent is made worse." And Paul begs the church at Corinth "that there be no divisions among you," the same word. So the Bible itself treats a schism as a wound. What tore in 1054? Two things, mostly. First, authority. The bishop of Rome said he spoke for the whole church, as successor of Peter. The Eastern bishops honored Rome as first among equals, but not as a ruler over them. Second, a single word in the creed. Over the centuries, Western churches had added a Latin word, filioque, and the Son, to the line about the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father. The East said nobody had the right to change a creed agreed at a council, and that the change blurred something true about God. There were smaller quarrels too: leavened or unleavened bread, beards, fasting days. Historians now say 1054 was less a single day than a long drifting apart: different languages, different empires, and neither side trying very hard to understand the other. The worst blow came later, in 1204, when Western crusaders sacked Constantinople itself. There were faults on both sides, and churches on both sides now say so. In 1965, Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras formally lifted the excommunications of 1054. They didn't end the split. But they took the paper off the altar.
screen: `SCHISMA: A TEAR IN THE CLOTH.` · `AUTHORITY, AND ONE WORD IN THE CREED.` · `A LONG DRIFT, THEN 1204.` · `1965: THE PAPER LIFTED.` · then, large: `THAT THERE BE NO DIVISIONS AMONG YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of a tear. Maybe in your family, a friendship, a church. Something that split years ago and was never quite mended. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to decide who was right. Just notice where it still aches. Notice that both sides probably had a piece of the fault. If you pray, you can pray for reconciliation, between the churches of East and West, and in the tear you're thinking of. If you don't pray, just hold both sides in mind, gently, at the same time. The bell holds the time.
Schism. From the Greek for a tear in cloth. A split in the church, like the one between East and West.
Your line: the split still aches. Today, take one small step toward a tear in your own life: a message, a kind word, or just letting go of who was right. Day two hundred eighty-six.

287.hook: icons, incense, the Divine Liturgy and becoming like God by grace

segments.voice: Yesterday, 1054: a paper on the altar, and a schism between East and West. Your line was the split still aches. Did you take one small step toward a tear of your own? Day two hundred eighty-seven.

An old chronicle from Kyiv tells a story. Around the year 987, Prince Vladimir sent envoys out to see how different peoples worshiped. When they came back from Constantinople, from the great church of Hagia Sophia, they could hardly describe it. They said, more or less: we didn't know whether we were in heaven or on earth. We only know that God dwells there among people. The gold, the singing, the incense rising through light from high windows. Soon after, Vladimir was baptized, and with him the people of Kyiv. Walk into an Orthodox church today, Greek, Russian, Romanian, Serbian, Ukrainian, and you may feel what those envoys felt. Candles flickering in front of painted faces. People kissing pictures. Almost everyone standing. Today's word is the name of that church.

Orthodoxy is Greek: orthos, right or straight, and doxa, which means both belief and glory. So Orthodoxy is right belief, and it's also right worship, right praise. Orthodox Christians would say you can't separate the two: what you believe is how you pray. The Orthodox Church is a family of self-governing churches, the patriarchates of Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem, and the churches of Russia, Greece, Romania, Serbia and more, sharing one faith and one communion, with no single head. Its main service is the Divine Liturgy, most often the one named for Saint John Chrysostom, sung almost entirely. Icons fill the church: Christ, Mary, the saints. When Orthodox Christians kiss an icon, they're not worshiping wood and paint. A council in 787 said the honor given to an image passes to the one it shows, the way you might kiss a photo of someone you love. And the goal of it all has a surprising name: theosis, becoming like God. It sounds bold, but it's rooted in a line from Second Peter, that we might be "partakers of the divine nature." Early church fathers put it even more strongly: God became human so that humans might share God's life. The Orthodox are careful here: not by nature, as if people turn into gods, but by grace, the way iron left in a fire glows with the fire's heat while staying iron. That's the whole arc of this week, by the way. One church, then many; the councils; the ancient churches of Africa and Asia; the road east; the tear of 1054; and now the church that says worship is heaven on earth.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a candle before an image. A holy picture if you have one, or a photograph of someone you love. If you can't light a real flame, picture one. Settle, and breathe. Look at the face in front of you. Let the honor you feel pass through the picture to the person it shows. If you pray, you can pray in the quiet, the way Orthodox Christians do before icons: silently, simply, eyes open. If you don't, just keep looking with love. The bell holds the time.
Orthodoxy. Right belief and right praise, from the Greek orthos and doxa. The church of icons and the Divine Liturgy.
Your line: heaven on earth. Today, notice one moment of beauty, a light, a song, a face, that makes you forget for a second where you are. Day two hundred eighty-seven.
